title: Thiou with Meat and Vegetables
author: Amina Savoura
desc: A tomato-red meat and vegetable stew, with turnips and carrots going in before the sweet potatoes, thickened with a splash of vinegar — served over separately boiled white rice.
longDesc: Thiou is the Senegalese stew you eat with rice, not a rice dish: the rice cooks separately and the sauce goes on top. Meat is browned in hot oil, onions are added and left until they turn pink, tomato concentrate and seeded fresh tomatoes cook five minutes, and a litre of water goes in for 25 minutes. Turnips and carrots go in next, and when they are almost cooked the potatoes and sweet potatoes follow with the remaining onions and garlic. A little pepper and vinegar are added and the sauce is left to thicken. The page’s tip is a small piece of sugar.
ingredients: 1 kg meat — kind not specified in the list
1 litre water, plus a little salt
A little vinegar — quantity not printed
A small piece of sugar (the page’s tip)
steps: Cut the meat into pieces, plunge them into hot oil and let them brown.
Add two chopped onions and let them go lightly pink.
Add the tomato concentrate and the fresh tomatoes, seeded and cut. Let simmer five minutes.
Pour in 1 litre of water and a little salt and simmer 25 minutes.
Add the turnips and carrots (cut into cubes or rounds) and the chile.
When these vegetables are almost cooked, add the potatoes and sweet potatoes cut into rounds, the remaining onions and the garlic.
Check the seasoning, adding pepper and a little vinegar, and let the sauce thicken.
Serve with white rice cooked separately.
chefTips: The structural cue is ‘when these vegetables are almost cooked’: turnips and carrots first, potatoes and sweet potatoes after, or the soft ones fall apart.
A small piece of sugar and a splash of vinegar are the page’s two unusual finishing touches.
Browned meat, pink onions and a thickened sauce are the visual cues; the page prints only two times.
Cook the rice separately — this is a stew, not a one-pot rice.
commonMistakes: Adding all the vegetables at once.
Cooking the rice in the sauce.
healthBenefits: Root vegetables give fibre and beta-carotene.
culturalNote: Aïssatou Mbaye calls thiou ‘moins célèbre que le yassa ou le mafé’, and says her own thiou sauces are light, close to the sauce of thiéré. It is the clean contrast with ceebu jen and ceebu yapp, where the rice finishes in the sauce.
sources: Title as printed: ‘Thiou à la viande’. Publication: Afrik (afrik.com). Date as printed: ‘Publié le 8 décembre 2012 à 22h18, mis à jour le 17 janvier 2025 à 23h28’. Yield: ‘Ingrédients (6 personnes)’. No preparation or cooking time fields; the only ‘2 min’ on the page is a reading time. TWO-PASS on quantities and method; both agree on every quantity.

BYLINE DISAGREEMENT, unreconciled: pass one read the byline as ‘Amina Savoura’ (consistent with every other Afrik recipe in this collection); pass two reported ‘Source: Afrik, recipe by Binebine’. Likely a page byline plus an in-body recipe credit, but no pass showed both at once. Both recorded; neither picked.
The meat kind is not printed in the ingredient list (a gloss of ‘beef or lamb’ in pass one is not on the page). Dried chile and pepper have no quantity; vinegar has none either.
Printed oddities kept: ‘rossir’ (here; the same author prints ‘rosir’ elsewhere), ‘les tomates fraîche’, ‘1 lite d’eau’, ‘les pommes de terres’.

Cues in short fragments: ‘laisser dorer’; ‘laisser rossir un peu’; ‘Quand ces légumes sont presque cuits’; ‘laisser la sauce épaissir’. Times printed: ‘cinq minutes’ and ‘25mn’ only. Prep and cook times in this entry are editorial estimates.

A separate au-senegal.com thiou page (organisation byline) prints almost the same structure with 1.5 litres of water and 5 tomatoes, one cooking time, and uses dried fish and vinegar without listing them; it was not published as its own entry.
